$comment: The engine-neutrality ratchet. One entry per directory under src/, recording how much of it
still names a JavaScript engine directly. scripts/check-engine-neutrality.sh measures the tree
and compares it against these numbers.
THESE NUMBERS MAY FALL AND MAY NEVER RISE. A count above its budget fails the build, and the
fix is to port the file rather than to raise the number. A migration that moves a file onto
Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal lowers a count, and must lower the budget in the SAME COMMIT -- the
check reports every count that came in under budget for exactly that reason, because a ratchet
nobody tightens is a ratchet that stops at whatever the worst day was.
THE ONE RISE THAT IS NOT A REGRESSION IS A CHANGE TO THE METRIC, AND THERE HAS BEEN ONE.
engineReferences used to count only the string 'Broiler.JavaScript'. Every project under src/
has a RootNamespace beginning 'Broiler.', so 'JavaScript.Runtime.JSObject' compiles and means
the same thing -- and 23 real references in Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom were spelled that way,
invisible to the check, concentrated in exactly the files mid-migration where somebody had
dropped a using and qualified what was left. The count now sees both spellings. Dom's recorded
number therefore went 108 -> 111 in the commit that widened it while its actual coupling FELL by
18 in the same commit, and both halves of that sentence are the point: a number may rise when
the instrument improves, and it may never rise because the tree got worse. A commit doing the
first says so here.
The consequence worth stating plainly: a project whose budget is already 0 cannot gain an
engine-coupled file at all. That is the state every entry here is travelling towards, and it
is what lets the remaining migration land as a hundred small changes instead of one merge that
moves 250 files and can only be reviewed by trusting it.
Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal is 0/0/0 and is the one entry these numbers do not actually protect.
Its project file has no ProjectReference and no PackageReference, so an assembly that cannot
see a Broiler.JavaScript type cannot name one: its neutrality is a compiler outcome, not a grep
result. What the check guards there is the CLAIM -- it fails if that project file ever gains a
reference of either kind, because the moment it does, every 0 below stops meaning anything.
WHAT EACH METRIC COUNTS, LITERALLY.
engineReferences   Occurrences of the text 'Broiler.JavaScript' in .cs files beneath the
directory, bin/ and obj/ excluded. Text, not semantics: a using directive,
a fully-qualified type name and a mention inside a doc comment each count
one. Counting occurrences rather than files is deliberate -- a file being
half-ported is progress, and a metric that only moved when a whole file
landed would hide it.
engineProjectRefs  ProjectReference Include paths in the directory's .csproj files that point
into Broiler.JS/ or Broiler.VM/, counted regardless of Condition. This is
the metric that actually has to reach 0 for an engine to be swappable: as
long as a binding project links the engine, nothing stops the next file
from using it, and the two counts above are the only thing noticing.
guestEvalSites     Occurrences of '.Eval(' in .cs files. The name records where these are
going, not what they are: today's sites are undifferentiated, and splitting
them into IJsSource.EvaluateHostScript (source this repository authored,
exempt from the page's content policy) and EvaluateClassicScript (a script
the page carries, which script-src governs) is the porting work this number
measures for a binding's sites; a provider's own evaluation and Dom's module
probe are counted as well and are not that work (see their notes). None goes to
EvaluateDynamicSource (what the page asks to evaluate at run time, which
'unsafe-eval' governs): no counted site evaluates text the page asks for at run
time, and the page's own eval and Function are refused inside the realm rather
than through that member. A ported site no longer names .Eval(, so it leaves
this count; engineReferences counts namespace text, so it falls only when a
port also deletes a using or qualified name the file no longer needs.
WHY THE UNIT IS A DIRECTORY AND NOT A PROJECT FILE. src/Broiler.App has no .csproj: its eight
files are pulled in by <Compile Include="..\Broiler.App\..."> from three heads. Keying this
on project files would leave those files counted nowhere, which is the one place an engine
reference could be parked without any budget noticing. Keying on the directory covers them, and
makes the entry name the same string the check prints.
This is an object rather than the array eng/solutions.json uses, so that a directory cannot be
budgeted twice -- two entries for one project would let the check read whichever came first.

A project marked "role": "provider" is the one kind whose engine references are SUPPOSED to grow -- naming the engine is what a provider assembly is for. For those, engineReferences and guestEvalSites are recorded and reported when they drift, but not enforced; engineProjectRefs stays enforced, because which engine assemblies a provider links is a real boundary and a Broiler.JS provider quietly acquiring a Broiler.VM reference should have to argue for it in a diff.

MOVED OUT OF Broiler.Browser ON 2026-09-16, WITH THE CODE IT BUDGETS. Seven entries went away in that move and none of them was a project this ratchet was ever about: Broiler.App, Broiler.App.Android, Broiler.Browser.Android, Broiler.Browser.Core, Broiler.Browser.Core.Tests, Broiler.Browser.Linux and Broiler.Browser.Windows. Six of the seven were at 0/0/0 and stayed in the browser; the seventh, Broiler.Browser.Core, carries one unconditional Broiler.JavaScript.All reference because BrowserApp.NewScriptEngine() still picks an engine with an #if rather than through JsEngineRegistry. That is now a fact about an EMBEDDER rather than about the bridge, which is the right place for it to be argued, and it is no longer measured here because this check deliberately does not look outside its own src/.

The engine ProjectReferences these numbers count are spelled $(BroilerJsRoot)/... and $(BroilerVmRoot)/... since the same move. The check knows both spellings and the relative one; scripts/check-engine-neutrality.sh says what it cost to find that out.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Core.note: ONE FILE, ONE LINE, AND IT IS THE SEAM. The single reference is `using Broiler.JavaScript.Engine;` in Dom/IDomBridgeRuntime.cs, and the only thing it serves is the pair of Attach overloads that take a JSContext. This was 3 across two files until ScriptCompileAhead.cs was deleted -- 327 lines with no caller anywhere in the tree, whose two usings were the other 2. What that removal buys is not the count: it means engineProjectRefs 1, the ProjectReference to Broiler.JavaScript.Engine, is now held by exactly one API in one file, so an Attach that takes an IJsRealm drops the reference in the same commit rather than turning up a second dependency behind it. This is the highest-value entry in the file despite being the smallest -- an Attach a second engine can call is what makes a second engine able to serve a page at all. Note for whoever ports it: Broiler.JS's own docs/roadmap/Modernization.md MOD-M5 names the deleted file as an import source, so it is taken from this repository's history rather than from the tree.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom.note: 27 -> 13, THE LISTENER RECORD, AND THE SEVEN-REFERENCE CONVERTER NO QUALIFIED GREP COULD SEE. EventListenerRegistration in DomBridge/RuntimeStates.cs held its listener as the engine value type, not the function type, so Features/EventListenerBinding.cs was engine-typed, and every binding reached it through a host member that converted a handle first: ToEngineListenerValue in DomBridge/DomBridge.WindowEventTargetHost.cs, which unwrapped an object and minted an engine null, boolean, number, string or undefined for anything else. All seven of that file's occurrences were spelled without the root, so the largest single concentration in the project read as clean to a grep for the qualified namespace. The record is a JsValue now. The converter is deleted, and so are the registration members of the element, document, window and messaging host contracts that led to it: the four bindings call EventListenerBinding directly with their call frame's realm, which is what IDocumentEventTargetHost's own remark said would happen when the record moved. The shared invoker in DomBridge/Events.cs calls a listener through the realm, in the shape the inline on* handler was already fired in, and MessagingBinding reads an on-type handler through the realm too. NOTHING A PAGE CAN SEE CHANGES, AND THE ONE COERCION THAT COULD HAVE IS WHY IJsValues.ToBoolean LANDED FIRST: a handle's AsBoolean is true for 0n, the engine coercion said false, and addEventListener(t, f, 0n) stays capture-false because the realm answers it. Measured with the check's own two patterns, per file: DomBridge/DomBridge.WindowEventTargetHost.cs 7 -> 0; DomBridge/Events.cs 3 -> 0; DomBridge/RuntimeStates.cs 1 -> 0; Features/EventListenerBinding.cs 2 -> 0; Features/MessagingBinding.cs 1 -> 0. DomBridge/RuntimeStates.cs reaches zero here, because the inline on* map in the same file had already left the engine using it shared with this record. 30 -> 27, THE INLINE on* HANDLER MAP, AND THE FILE IT WAS SAID TO BE WAITING ON WAS NEVER THE CONSTRAINT. InlineStyleRuntimeState.InlineEventHandlers in DomBridge/RuntimeStates.cs was a dictionary of the engine's value type, and four comments in four files gave one reason for keeping it so: the map lives in a file this round does not own. Every read and write of it goes through DomBridge.GetInlineEventHandlers, and every caller of that is in three files -- DomBridge/Events.cs compiling an on* attribute, DomBridge.EventDispatchHost.cs firing one, DomBridge/DomBridge.EventHandlerReflectorHost.cs reflecting element.onclick -- each already holding a JSEAL handle and converting only at the map: an unwrap at both writers, a wrap at both readers. The map holds handles now and all four conversions are gone (JsInterop. occurrences over this project 28 -> 23). Per file, both spellings: DomBridge.EventDispatchHost.cs 1 -> 0 and DomBridge/DomBridge.EventHandlerReflectorHost.cs 1 -> 0, each losing the using its one type test needed; DomBridge.cs 2 -> 1, because the wrapper-root fields that shared its Runtime using were re-typed first; DomBridge/RuntimeStates.cs 1 -> 1, because its using is also held by EventListenerRegistration, and the commit that re-types the record takes it; DomBridge/Events.cs 3 -> 3, its three usings being InvokeEventListener's. NOTHING A PAGE CAN SEE CHANGES: both writers store only a handle that answered IsFunction, the provider and the seam both give an engine function kind Function, and a handle compares kind and then reference, so each reader now returns the stored handle where it used to mint an equal one. onclick === onclick and onclick === f are the engine's own identity either way, and EventListenerRegistrationTests now asserts both, and that an assigned and a setAttribute handler each fire -- none of which anything asserted. 34 -> 33 BY DELETING AN OVERLOAD THE PLAN CALLED DEAD AND THAT HAD TWO LIVE CALLERS. (This heading said 36 -> 35, and the crossings figure below said 55 -> 53, as does that commit's message: both were measured in a copy of the tree that did not yet have the customElements commit, 36 -> 34, under it. The moves were right; the ends were not, and they are corrected here.) DomBridge/WrapperPrototypes.cs carried two LinkToInterface overloads, one over a handle and one over the engine's object, and the remarks above the engine-typed one named five files as the callers it existed to gather: the two wrapper factories DomBridge/JsObjects.cs and its non-element sibling, DomBridge/CharacterDataInterface.cs, DomBridge/Registration/Registration.cs and DomBridge.AttributesHost.cs, all of which it said mint a wrapper as the engine's object and are other groups' files this round. An untruncated grep for the name finds fourteen occurrences in the whole repository, every one of them inside this project, and THREE OF THOSE FIVE FILES DO NOT CONTAIN ONE. The factories and the character-data file call ApplyInterfacePrototype instead, with a handle the realm minted -- JsObjects.cs:92-95 is Realm.NewExotic or Realm.NewObject and line 103 is the call -- and all three measure zero engine references, so they are nobody's files this round either. The overload had exactly two callers and both were round trips: Registration.cs:226 passed documentObject, which is ToEngineObject(document) taken 95 lines earlier for the _documentJSObject field, and DomBridge.AttributesHost.cs:41 unwrapped the handle its own interface member had just been handed. FromEngineObject on the callee's single line undid each conversion. Both call sites now pass the handle they hold, and the deletion cannot hide a missed one: JsValue declares no conversion operator and JSObject cannot declare one because Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal has no project reference for it to name, so any surviving engine-typed argument is a compile error rather than a silent rebind. THE METRIC MOVES BY ONE AND IT IS A using LINE. WrapperPrototypes.cs 1 -> 0, its whole coupling having been the namespace of a parameter type. Registration.cs stays at 2 and DomBridge.AttributesHost.cs measured 0 before and after, because a JsInterop crossing names no engine type -- the same blind spot several entries above already record. Crossings over src/ go 54 -> 52 by grep -rno "JsInterop[.]" --include=*.cs src/ | wc -l. AND A COMMENT IN A FILE WITH NO ENGINE REFERENCE AT ALL: DomBridge.AttributesHost.cs said the wrapper is unwrapped to the engine object the bridge's prototype table is keyed on. There is no prototype table. The phrase occurs exactly once in the repository, in that sentence; LinkToInterface reads the interface constructor off the realm's global and installs the prototype through IJsMembers.SetPrototype, and no table is consulted anywhere on the path. NEITHER RE-TYPED SITE HAS A TEST. Nothing under src/Broiler.Browser.Core.Tests names Attr as a word, getAttributeNode, createAttribute or HTMLDocument; the one constructor.name assertion over DOM wrappers, DomEnumerationAndArityTests.ADomObjectReportsItsKindAndItsInterface, reads div.constructor.name and document.body.constructor.name, which reach the surviving handle overload through ApplyInterfacePrototype's re-link sweep and never reached the deleted one. 44 -> 43 BY DELETING ANOTHER MEMBER HELD OPEN BY A DOC COMMENT NAMING A CALLER IT DID NOT HAVE. DomBridge.WindowContext.cs carried two RunWithWindowContext overloads, one taking the engine's object and one taking a handle, and the remarks above them said the engine-typed one was kept for the sub-document script runner in DomBridge/SubDocuments.cs. That call site is one unchanged line and it has bound to the handle overload ever since SubWindowBinding.GetOrCreate was re-typed to answer one -- FrameScriptExecutionTests was written to cover precisely that rebinding and says so in its header, so the tree carried its own disproof in a second file. The only caller the engine-typed overload actually had was DomBridge.MessagingHost.cs, which unwrapped a handle to an engine object so the overload could wrap the same object straight back before handing it to WindowContextManager, whose single RunWithWindowContext has taken a handle all along. The round trip was unobservable and that is checkable rather than assumed: both callers of IMessagingHost.RunWithWindowContext are guarded to objects (MessagingBinding.RunInOwnerWindow returns early unless IsObject, and WindowPostMessage falls back to the installed window handle when call.This is not one), and JsInterop.FromEngineObject now answers the kind the provider would, so the trip was identity in reference and in kind for every value that could reach it. One occurrence moves, in one file: the using line the deleted parameter needed. DomBridge.WindowContext.cs 1 -> 0, and JsInterop. crossings 93 -> 91. 49 -> 48, AND THE ONE OCCURRENCE THAT WENT WAS A using LINE THAT EIGHTEEN CALL SITES IN FIFTEEN OTHER FILES WERE KEEPING ALIVE. FindDomNodeByJSObject and FindDomElementByJSObject in DomBridge/Utilities.cs took the engine's object; every caller held a JSEAL handle, unwrapped it at its own seam, and the pair wrapped it straight back up to ask a registry that has been keyed on JsValue.ObjectIdentity since it was re-typed. Both now take the handle. That deleted 19 JsInterop crossings (97 -> 78 by grep -o) and left fifteen files with none at all, but the ratchet could only ever see the one using -- which is the same lesson Runtime/JsInterop.cs records and the reason 49 falls by 1 and not by 19. The names still spell the type they no longer take; renaming them moves no count and is a separate change. TWO THROWS STOP HAPPENING, NOT ONE, AND THEY ARE UNREACHABLE FOR DIFFERENT REASONS. JsInterop.ToEngineObject is `ReferenceOf(value) as JSObject ?? throw`, and its own doc comment names both causes: a primitive, or a handle from a realm of another engine. (a) THE PRIMITIVE. Eight of the eighteen sites have no IsObject guard of their own, and all eight are called only from module frames that do guard, verified caller by caller, so no page reaches the old throw or the new null. (b) THE FOREIGN REALM. Under a non-Broiler.JS realm every one of the eighteen throws today whatever the guards say, because `as JSObject` is null for a handle another engine minted; after this commit they resolve through JsObjectRegistry by ObjectIdentity, which is engine-neutral. THAT IS PROGRESS TOWARD A SECOND ENGINE AND NOT A SECOND ENGINE: the bridge still refused one earlier, in the ToEngineObject calls inside Attach that fed the wrapper roots and the two registration hubs still taking the engine's object -- which were never the keystone's to remove, and go with the roots and those hubs rather than with the Attach signature. Claiming this commit makes the VM profile able to host a DOM would be exactly the overreach the plan warns against. 111 UNDER A WIDER METRIC THAN THE 108 IT REPLACES, AND THE TREE GOT BETTER, NOT WORSE. The count now also sees engine namespaces spelled without their Broiler. root -- 23 of them here -- while the same commit deleted 20 dead using lines from the four LayoutMetrics partials and added 2 that JsInterop needs to answer the kind a provider would. Real coupling fell by 18. The DOM bridge. Started at 891 when JSEAL landed, and the name-validation cluster moved -- ThrowDOMException and the three validators now take an IJsRealm and reach IJsCalls.DomError, which the Broiler.JS provider implements with the same algorithm and the same fallback wording, so no page sees a different exception. That commit also removed IAttributesHost.JsContext, whose own doc comment had named the condition for its removal. What remains is structural rather than unmigrated: IDomBridgeRuntime.Attach, which takes a JSContext from another project; BridgeModuleContext, which derives from the engine's module context because JSEAL has no module-graph contract. (This clause also named the listener record and the inline on* handler map that DomBridge/RuntimeStates.cs declares, as holding a listener and an inline handler as the engine's value type. Both hold handles now: the map since 30 -> 27 and the record since 27 -> 13. And it said the event-host surfaces still type a listener as the engine's function. Nothing in the bridge does: the last store that did was the visual-viewport list, re-typed at 33 -> 30.) The weak tables that were recorded here as needing a reference-typed key a struct handle cannot be were a MISTAKE: the struct was never the key, the reference it carries is, and JsValue.ObjectIdentity carried five of them across with no provider change. The ArrayBuffer mint left when IJsValues grew NewArrayBuffer and TryGetArrayBufferBytes, and the Storage delete left when IJsExoticDelete landed -- both were contract gaps rather than unmigrated code, and both closed by adding to JSEAL rather than by working around it here. Each occurrence names its own pin in its doc comment. 60 -> 49 BY DELETION RATHER THAN PORTING, and the shape of what went is the point: four members with no caller anywhere in the tree, two of which carried a doc comment naming the caller they did not have -- IEventTargetHost.DispatchEventOnElement(DomNode, JSObject), the in-Arguments overload of StartSubDocumentViewTransition with its OptionsHandle, and TraversalBinding.GetSelection. Plus three dead locals that no metric could see at all, because a JsInterop crossing names no engine type. 42 -> 39, THE TIMER PATH, AND THE PAIR OF COMMENTS THAT KEPT IT. Dom.Features.TimerBinding narrowed every setTimeout/setInterval/requestAnimationFrame callback to the engine's function type, and Runtime/BrowserEventLoop.cs carried three engine-typed overloads that wrapped the same reference straight back into the handle it had arrived as. Each side's doc comment named the other as its reason: the binding said the loop's queues hold the engine's own function type and that this is not part of the migration, the loop said the binding still narrows and is another group's file this round. The first was false when it was written -- TimerEntry.Fn is a JsValue, _rafCallbacks is a map of them, the no-callback test is already !callback.IsFunction, and the drain already invokes through the realm accessor the loop is constructed with -- and the second miscounted its own adapters as two when there are three. JsValue compares kind and then reference, and the Broiler.JS provider mints kind Function only for a JSFunction, so the round trip was the identity on the handle and deleting it changes nothing a page can see. The three references were 2 in TimerBinding.cs and 1 using line in BrowserEventLoop.cs, and the 2 are why a qualified per-file grep read TimerBinding as zero: they are spelled JavaScript.BuiltIns.Function.JSFunction with no Broiler. root, which is exactly the spelling the widened metric exists to see. Neither file names an engine type now. THE CLAUSE ABOUT JsObjectRegistry BEING THE WRAPPER-IDENTITY CHOKE POINT IS DELETED HERE: that file was re-typed onto JsValue and measures zero, and three separate investigations quoted this note as their scope statement and inherited the error. 64 -> 60 and 6 -> 5 by deleting rather than porting: DomFunction, superseded when the Broiler.JS provider took createPrototype:false for every member the bridge installs, so its 3 references were paying for a type nothing constructed; a stale using in ElementContentBinding that named the engine and used nothing from it; and RegisterNamedElementGlobals, public, JSContext-typed, carrying one of the eval sites, and with no caller at any point in this repository's history. NOTE FOR ANYONE WRITING PROSE ABOUT THIS METRIC: guestEvalSites is textual and a mention in a comment counts as a call, so the first attempt at DomBridge.cs's replacement comment held the count at 6 by naming the method it was describing. That is the metric working as specified, not a bug in it. guestEvalSites 5 -> 1, in two commits: the three sub-document classic-script loops in SubDocuments.cs and then the XHTML one in SubDocuments.XmlAndScripts.cs now go through IJsSource.EvaluateClassicScript rather than the engine's own evaluation entry point. engineReferences does not move: SubDocuments.XmlAndScripts.cs had none, and SubDocuments.cs's one is a using for the module tail below those loops, which still needs a JSModuleContext the source contract does not describe. THE REMAINING 1 IS NOT A LEFTOVER OF THESE PORTS: it is EngineModuleSupport.cs's probe, reading back a number the module stored on a BridgeModuleContext the method builds itself, and the module run it reads stays engine-typed until JSEAL has a module contract. A commit taking this to 0 should say whether it moved that read onto an adopted realm or did something else. 38 -> 36, AND THE PIN THE COMMENT RECORDED DID NOT EXIST. window.frames was built with the engine's array type, and the header comment on DomBridge.WindowLoad.cs gave the reason as its caller -- DomBridge/Registration/Window.cs, which 'takes the engine's array'. It does not: it converted that array back to a handle on the line it received it, so the reference bought a round trip and nothing else. Minting the array with realm.NewArray deletes both halves at once -- one using line, which this metric sees, and two seam crossings, which it does not. It also removes the last converting caller of SubWindowBinding.GetOrCreate, whose own doc comment named that caller as the reason it need not convert, so a second comment describing a pin that had already stopped existing. DomBridge.WindowLoad.cs goes 2 -> 0, and its two using lines are the whole move. (This said 3 -> 2 and NOT to zero, that the two namespaces left were the ones DispatchWindowEvent's parameter and return types are spelled in, and it counted one using line where two went. The 45 -> 44 commit had already taken the file from 3 to 2, and both remaining usings went here.) 45 -> 44 BY DELETING ONE using LINE, AND THE DEPENDENCY IT NAMED WAS NEVER LOAD-BEARING. DispatchWindowEvent in DomBridge.WindowLoad.cs answered the engine boolean over the engine object, and its doc comment named IWindowEventTargetHost, ILocationHost, DomBridge.MessagingHost.cs and DomBridge/LayoutMetrics.Scrolling.cs as the files that pinned those two types. All four were wrong: the three contracts have declared DispatchWindowEvent(JsValue) since they were extracted, the fourth calls the string overload and throws the answer away, and of the seven call sites the two overloads have between them exactly one reads the return value -- and it converted it to a handle on the same line. The engine object was minted by three bridge-side adapters for no reader but the parameter they were said to pin. One pin was real and it is a call site: InvokeEventListener takes the engine object because EventListenerRegistration is engine-typed in DomBridge/RuntimeStates.cs, so that crossing moved out of three callers into one conversion at the top of the method, taken before the guard so a handle carrying no engine object still fails exactly where it failed before. JsInterop. crossings fall by one on net: three go and one arrives. 48 -> 45, AND THE THIRD ONE WAS NOT PREDICTED. Three files reach 0 here -- DomBridge/LayoutMetrics.Scrolling.cs, Features/TableBinding.cs and Features/FormAssociationBinding.cs -- because in each of them the single counted occurrence was the using line that five deleted members needed. The plan for this commit expected -2, on the ground that LayoutMetrics.Scrolling.cs stays pinned by DispatchVisualViewportScrollEvent. It does not: that method reads the wrapper root through var, and var infers without a using. A SEMANTIC PIN AND A COUNTED REFERENCE ARE NOT THE SAME THING, and this file only ever had the second. NOTHING DELETED HERE WAS DEAD, which is the other half of the shape. Each of the five members had exactly one caller, and each caller reached it by converting a JSEAL handle it already held into the engine object so the callee could convert it straight back: DomBridge/DomBridge.ElementGeometryHost.cs:67,103 for the three scroll-option adapters and DomBridge/ElementInterfaces.cs:103,107,128 for the two installers. Four conversions and five adapters, deleted together, no behaviour anywhere between them. AND THREE COMMENTS DIED WITH THEM, EACH NAMING A CALLER IT DID NOT HAVE. The scroll readers were "shared by every scrolling entry point the bridge has" when their only caller was the element-geometry contract -- the window and sub-window contracts read their own options through a second, static copy in DomBridge.SubWindowHost.cs. The same comment argued the readers cannot be static because "a static has no way to obtain" the realm, which that static pair does by taking it as a parameter. And DomBridge/ElementInterfaces.cs opened on "the two engine namespaces left" while having none, and having had none since ComputedStyleBinding migrated. 43 -> 42 BY DELETING AN ADAPTER THAT HAD ALREADY LOST ITS REASON, AND THE REASON IS WORTH READING TWICE. EventTargetRegistry.TryGetOwnerWindow answered the engine's object over a map that has been keyed on JsValue since the listener stores were re-typed, and the doc comment defending that signature said its one caller held an engine object on both sides of the call. WindowContextManager has taken and answered a handle since the commit BEFORE the one that wrote that sentence, so it was false on the day it was written: the accessor unwrapped the caller's handle, minted a second handle over the same object to look the entry up under, and unwrapped the stored window so the caller could wrap it again -- four crossings on a round trip whose two ends were already handles. The tree's JsInterop crossings go 62 -> 58. The reciprocal error was in WindowContextManager's own remarks, which named EventTargetRegistry as keying its maps on the engine's object: true when written, falsified by the commit that re-typed those maps, never updated, and each file's comment was the other's justification. AND THE SEAM HAS NEVER HAD A TEST. ResolveOwnerWindow falls back to ResolveCurrentWindow() on a miss, so on a page with one window the map's answer and the map's absence are the same window and deleting the map outright would not turn a test red; a test that could fail here has to give the target an owner that DIFFERS from the current window, which in this bridge means a nested browsing context. Nothing under src/Broiler.Browser.Core.Tests named an owner window at all. (True when written: the next commit added OwnerWindowRoutingTests, whose port is created inside a frame's script and delivered from the page's post-load drain, so its owner and the current window differ and only the map can tell them apart.) 39 -> 38 BY REMOVING A PIN NEITHER CALLER SUPPLIED. RegisterWindowMessaging took a JSObject because its own remark said the parameter was pinned twice over by two callers that both hand this the engine's window object. Neither did: DomBridge/Registration/Window.cs holds realm.Global and unwrapped it on the argument line, Features/SubWindowBinding.cs mints its window through the realm and unwrapped that, and the method's own first statement wrapped the object straight back up -- three conversions round-tripping one object, held in place by a sentence asserting a fact about two other files, which is the same failure mode as the four members deleted at 60 -> 49. The metric moves by one because one using line goes; the crossings it cannot see move by two, 55 -> 53 over this directory excluding Runtime/JsInterop.cs's own prose. The same file's class remark named FOUR collaborators still holding a JS object as an engine value; two of the four were already wrong when it was read -- the event-target registry keys its owner map on JsValue, and LocationBinding is built from a realm and a string and never receives the window at all -- and this leaves ONE, the sub-window map in Runtime/BrowsingContextManager.cs, which is what the surviving unwrap in SubWindowBinding is for. 36 -> 34, AND THE FILE REACHED ZERO ON A PIN THE PLAN EXPECTED TO HOLD IT OPEN. RegisterCustomElements took (JSContext, JSObject) and read neither parameter. The context was defended in writing -- its doc comment said the parameter stays only so that call site needs no edit while it is another group's file -- and both halves of that were false: the call site is DomBridge/Registration/Registration.cs:224, which this commit edits anyway, and it is inside this migration group. The window was unwrapped on the one line that used it, realm.DefineValue(JsInterop.FromEngineObject(window), ...), against a caller holding realm.Global, so the engine type bought a single round trip and no capability. Both parameters go, both using lines go with them, and DomBridge/Registration/CustomElements.cs measures 0 by both spellings -- 2 -> 0, not 2 -> 1. The plan said 35 and said the file would keep a pin at :240, where DocumentValue reads _documentJSObject. That read is `is { } main`, a pattern variable: it names no namespace, so this metric has never counted it, and re-typing the field (the commit that owns :240) will move the metric by nothing here. A semantic pin and a counted reference are different things, and this is the second file in this migration predicted to stay pinned that measured zero. DomBridge/Registration/Registration.cs contributes nothing to the fall: its two references are JSContext for the code-cache swap and DictionaryCodeCache itself, both untouched, and its own header comment -- which had listed the custom-elements hub as a reason the window conversion had to stay -- is corrected in the same commit rather than left to justify the next signature. 33 -> 33: THE THREE WRAPPER ROOTS ARE HANDLES, AND THE -1 THE PLAN GAVE THIS COMMIT WAS ALREADY SPENT. DomBridge.cs held document, window and visualViewport as the engine's own object type, and every reader wrapped them straight back into a handle; they are the handles the realm minted now, under the names the migrated readers already used -- DocumentHandle, WindowHandle, VisualViewportHandle -- and the engine-typed fields are gone. The plan's -1 was DomBridge/LayoutMetrics.Scrolling.cs reaching zero here; it reached zero at 48 -> 45, for the reason that entry gives: its visualViewport dispatch read the root through var. Nothing counted moves. Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.note: Proved by the compiler, not by this file. The project has no ProjectReference and no PackageReference, so it cannot name an engine type whatever a grep says; the check fails if that project file ever gains one. See the comment in Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.csproj.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.BroilerJs.note: The Broiler.JS provider, and the one project under src/ whose budget is not expected to reach zero. Naming Broiler.JavaScript is what this assembly is for: every reference here is a reference the bridge no longer has to make. The single eval site is JSContext.Eval inside the realm's own IJsSource implementation -- the provider being asked to evaluate, not a binding evaluating. Its engine project references were Broiler.JavaScript.Engine and .BuiltIns until IJsClone landed and took engineProjectRefs from 2 to 3: JSGlobalStatic.StructuredClone lives in Broiler.JavaScript.Globals, so the provider that implements structured clone needs it. That is the gate doing its job rather than a regression -- the same reference LEFT Broiler.HtmlBridge.Dom in the same commit, because the bridge's only use of it was the call that is now behind the contract. An engine assembly reached by the provider and not by the bridge is the shape all of these should end in.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Jseal.Vm.note: The Broiler.VM provider. It is marked a provider for the same reason the Broiler.JS one is - naming an engine is what a provider is FOR - but its reference count reads 0 rather than a large number, and the zero is a fact about the METRIC and not about this assembly. engineReferences counts occurrences of the string Broiler.JavaScript, which is the Broiler.JS engine namespace; this provider names Broiler.VM.Profile.JavaScript instead, so the count does not see it. The five project references do see it, and they are the honest measure here: Abstractions, Binary, Runtime, the profile, and the profile compiler. Read the 0 as "this assembly names no Broiler.JS type", which is true and worth keeping true, and read the 5 as its engine coupling.

Broiler.HtmlBridge.Scripting.note: Five files now: the Broiler.JS ScriptEngine and what it needs to build a realm. InteractiveSession left the count when its constructor stopped taking a JSContext -- it read the context once, to dispose it, so the parameter is typed IDisposable and the class names no engine type at all. That reference was load-bearing for a reason unrelated to what it did: VmScriptEngine named the constructor as half of why the document-bearing overloads are forwarded. This is where the Broiler.JS provider will live once it is one, and the counts here move to a Jseal.BroilerJs assembly rather than to zero -- a provider naming its own engine is what a provider is for.
